paper: Sethian 1996, A fast marching level set method for monotonically advancing fronts, PNAS 93(4):1591-1595
verdict_context: REPLICATED at algorithm level; C1/C3 supported, C2 partial on singular point source (rate ~0.73), bit-exact on smooth plane-wave data

open_questions.q: Do higher-order upwind Godunov schemes (2nd- or 3rd-order ENO/WENO variants of the update in Eqn. 8/9) restore near-first-order convergence in anisotropic-speed regions, or does the source-point gradient blow-up still dominate the observed L-infinity rate?
open_questions.basis: Our C2 point-source experiment yielded rate ~0.73 with the paper's first-order Godunov update while the plane-wave (smooth) case was bit-exact. The paper does not test order in a family of speeds F(x,y), and higher-order upwind extensions (Sethian & Vladimirsky, Zhang et al.) postdate the paper. It is an open empirical question at what grid resolutions the higher-order scheme beats first-order in the presence of both a source singularity and an anisotropic F.
open_questions.next_steps: Implement a 2nd-order upwind update using the same heap/marching skeleton; rerun our C2 sweep (n in {33,65,...,513}) plus a smoothly-varying F(x,y)=1+0.5*sin(2*pi*x)*cos(2*pi*y) case; fit slopes; compare to the 0.73 baseline.

open_questions.q: How does patch-based / domain-decomposition parallel FMM (e.g. Herrmann; Yang & Stern) compare to the serial heap-based FMM at the crossover where our serial code hits its ~10 s wall-time at n=1025? Does the O(N log N) scaling survive across MPI ranks or does the causality-constraint of the marching order dominate?
open_questions.basis: Our C1 measurements are single-threaded serial (heapq on one CPU) up to N ~ 1e6. The paper's proof of O(N log N) is inherently serial: 'each cell is finalized exactly once' in ascending T order. Parallel FMM must relax this (patch reconciliation, restart on cross-boundary updates) and the effective work factor is not derivable from the paper.
open_questions.next_steps: Prototype a 2-D domain-decomposed FMM with 4 and 16 patches; measure runtime on n in {513, 1025, 2049} and total work (heap operations, cross-boundary re-updates). Compare to serial. Instrument re-update count as a function of speed contrast.

open_questions.q: Can the fast marching machinery be extended to Finsler (direction-dependent) geometries F(x, n_hat) without losing the O(N log N) complexity, or does the direction-dependence force iterative relaxation of the marching order?
open_questions.basis: Sethian 1996 assumes F(x,y) is isotropic (a scalar). The Godunov quadratic separates cleanly into axis-aligned differences precisely because of isotropy. Finsler generalizations (Sethian & Vladimirsky 2003 for anisotropy) require solving a small local optimization per cell and can revisit cells (breaking single-finalization). It is an open question in our replication whether Finsler-FMM retains N log N in practice on realistic anisotropy strengths.
open_questions.next_steps: Implement Sethian-Vladimirsky-style local nonlinear solve in place of _solve_quadratic; test on a Riemannian metric with modest anisotropy ratio (2:1, 5:1, 10:1); count re-updates per cell and fit the runtime vs N.

open_questions.q: For the same Eikonal problem, at what problem size does fast sweeping (Zhao 2005; Kao-Osher-Qian) outperform fast marching on modern CPUs, and does this crossover shift under our specific two-material speed field (C3) or high-contrast media?
open_questions.basis: The paper predates fast sweeping and does not compare. Our C3 test shows FMM handles the 2-material case with zero monotone violations, but does not benchmark alternatives. Fast sweeping has O(N) with a constant that depends on characteristic complexity; the crossover with heap-FMM's O(N log N) is problem-dependent and worth quantifying in our own harness.
open_questions.next_steps: Implement Gauss-Seidel fast sweeping in the same code base; rerun C1 grids and the C3 two-material problem; measure wall-time, iteration count until residual < 1e-10, and memory. Report the crossover N.

open_questions.q: In geometric-optics settings where characteristics cross (caustics / shocks in T), does our FMM implementation silently pick the first-arrival viscosity solution as the paper claims, or does the largest-root selection admit spurious multi-valued behavior in the accepted set?
open_questions.basis: The paper argues by monotonicity that the largest root is the viscosity-consistent update, so first-arrival time is recovered. We tested this only in cases where characteristics do not cross (single point source, plane-wave, and 2-material with source on the interface). We have no direct evidence for caustic behavior in our runs, so the claim is not falsified but also not tested.
open_questions.next_steps: Construct a two-source case with sources at (n/4,n/2) and (3n/4,n/2), F=1, n=513; the exact first-arrival T is min(r1,r2) with a caustic along x=n/2; compare our numerical T against min(r1,r2); measure error at the caustic. Also try F(x,y) with a Gaussian slow-down bump that focuses characteristics.
